d.title: Lloyd's algorithm, and the objective it is descending
d.caption: Each step can only lower the within-cluster sum of squares, so the algorithm converges — to a **local** minimum that depends on the start, which is why `n_init` exists. What it cannot do is change the objective: k-means always looks for the partition that minimises squared distance to a centre, and that is what makes it find round, similar-sized blobs whether or not the data has any.

items.desc: this step cannot increase the objective

Repeat until nothing moves

d.title: Five rules for k, and what each is blind to
d.caption: On the churn customers the elbow has **no bend**, the gap statistic **keeps rising**, and silhouette peaks at 0.29 — all three are telling you the same thing, which is that there are no clusters here, only a continuum. The last row is the only one that can say that out loud, and the last row is not a statistic.

d.title: Six clustering families, by the shape each can find
d.caption: The first column is the question people ask and the second is the one that decides the answer. DBSCAN finds any shape **at one density**, which is exactly why HDBSCAN replaced it as the default: real data has clusters at several densities, and a single eps cannot describe them.

d.title: The BIC that collapsed, and why it was not structure
d.caption: BIC fell off a cliff at five components — from 2,502 to −1,317 — and it means nothing. The discount column takes three values with 686 rows at zero, and two components had **variance 0.0000** on it: a Gaussian concentrated on a point mass has unbounded density there, so the likelihood is arbitrarily large. With a covariance floor of 0.1 the collapse disappears and leaves a shallow minimum at three.

d.title: Five questions about a clustering, and the index for each
d.caption: The first row is the trap: on the two moons, k-means scored a silhouette of **0.487** and the true labelling scored **0.328** — so the internal index preferred the wrong answer, because it measures the geometry a convex method produces rather than the structure that is there.

d.title: Why agreement must be corrected for chance
d.caption: Two random partitions of the same rows agree substantially just by accident, and the raw Rand index reports that agreement as skill. ARI subtracts the expected value under random labelling, which is why it can go negative — and why a plain Rand index of 0.7 says almost nothing.
cells: each class sits in one cluster

d.title: From 'maximise the variance' to an eigenproblem
d.caption: The derivation is short and it explains every property PCA has. Maximising the projected variance subject to a unit-length direction is a Lagrange problem whose stationary condition **is** the eigenvector equation — so the components are eigenvectors not by construction but by consequence, and their eigenvalues are the variances.

items.label: Centre the data
items.desc: the mean is subtracted; without this the first component points at the mean

items.label: Ask for the unit direction of maximum variance
Lagrange: Cw = lambda w
items.desc: the stationary condition is the eigenvector equation

items.label: So the variance along w is lambda
items.desc: the eigenvalue is the explained variance

items.label: Next direction, orthogonal to the first
items.desc: the second eigenvector, and so on

items.label: Equivalently, the SVD of the centred matrix
items.desc: which is how it is actually computed

d.title: The two claims PCA makes
d.caption: PCA asserts that the interesting directions are the **high-variance** ones and that the structure is **linear**. Nothing in the computation looks at the target, so a low-variance direction carrying all the signal is discarded without complaint — and no amount of components fixes a curved manifold.

d.title: PCA finds what varies; LDA finds what separates
d.caption: They can point in nearly opposite directions. If two classes differ along a low-variance axis, PCA throws that axis away and LDA keeps only it. LDA is supervised, which means it must be fitted inside the fold like any other label-using step.

d.title: What a t-SNE plot does and does not tell you
d.caption: It preserves neighbourhoods and negotiates away everything else. Cluster sizes here were stretched 4–14× **and in a different order**; between-cluster gaps correlate only 0.7 with the real ones; and pure Gaussian noise produced an embedding with a silhouette of 0.34. There is no `transform`, so a new point cannot be placed without re-running the whole embedding.

d.title: Random search beats grid search for a reason that is arithmetic
d.caption: A grid over 4 hyperparameters at 5 values each is 625 fits that try only **5 distinct values** of whichever parameter actually matters. Random search with the same budget tries 625 distinct values of each. The argument is strongest exactly when it matters most: when you do not know in advance which parameter is the important one.

d.title: Why the tuned score is biased, and what nested CV costs
d.caption: Taking the best of n cross-validated scores is taking the maximum of n noisy numbers, and the maximum of noise is positive. The inner loop chooses; the outer loop measures a procedure that includes the choosing. There is no way to get both from one loop.
